title: Courage and Blind Spots
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk explores how recognizing and understanding our own "blind spots" - both physical and conceptual - can lead to greater compassion and wisdom in our lives. By embracing the idea that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence, we can develop a more open and non-judgmental mind, allowing us to see things as they truly are rather than through our preconceptions. This understanding is closely tied to cultivating bodhicitta, or awakened heart, which involves a selfless desire for all beings to be happy and free from suffering.

sentences.text: Blind spots in a literal physical sense refer to, of course, a tiny spot in our vision just outward from the center of our vision and down a bit where we cannot see because that's where the optic nerve attaches to the retina.

Maybe in high school psychology class you tried the experiment where you have a piece of paper with two dots on it and if you hold the paper just right and look at one of the dots the other one disappears.
Our brain makes up and fills in the most likely visual information, which in our class we saw can be colors and even lines.
More generally, blind spots refer to anything we can't perceive, and moreover, we can't perceive that we can't perceive it.
For example, if we have motivations or assumptions about another person's motivations.
An important element of the analogy between the physical blind spot and the metaphorical one is that insidiousness of our brain filling in a likely substitute.
So it's not like there's missing information and we can say, "Oh, there's something missing there, I'll investigate and find out what it is."
No, the fact that information is missing is hidden from us.

In fact, it's very unlikely that anyone would come across the physical blind spot just by chance unless they happen to be playing with a piece of paper with two dots on it and looking at one but paying attention to the other dot.
We generally learn about this from a teacher or friend.
Similarly, we need help in identifying our metaphorical blind spots.
Recently, in an emergency service organization that I belong to, one of the board members, Denise, recently left the organization following a disagreement with a new board member, Jen.
This was quite notable because Denise had been a leader in the community for decades.
She is an educator and an innovator.
About four years ago, the leader of another emergency service organization made very bitter, very public accusations about the motives behind discipline that Denise was enforcing.

Denise was deeply hurt and broke off all communication with the other organization and has continued ever since to insist that no one from our organization will ever take direction from somebody in the other.
Now Jen comes along as a new board member and wants the two organizations to work together more closely.
Denise believes that Jen is being mean and disrespectful for pushing this painful path, and Jen believes that Denise is being selfish and unreasonable.
Where are the blind spots and where is the courage?
In multiple levels of our Zen community, there are now efforts underway to develop a more structured approach to resolving conflict.
Within the Red Cedar Zen community, we are working on adopting some guidelines and steps to offer for dealing with conflict.
And I understand that the many teachers from the various everyday Zen communities are working together on this.
And finally, the North American Soto Zen Association is studying what it can offer.
Now, to be clear, I believe that there are some major differences in the approaches.
At the local level, we're working on interpersonal everyday conflict.
And at the large level, the Soto Zen Association, I believe, is working on bringing to light serious lapses in ethical conduct that Norman was talking about this morning and how do we handle those.
Both really need to be a part of the conflict that we study and that we have the courage to face.
The study of blind spots and courage fits squarely in with the study of conflict.

It's rare to find conflict without also finding the serious inability of each side to conceive the possibility that the other has a valid worldview, much less be able to imagine what that worldview is.
The koans we studied in the practice period classes come from the record of the hidden lamp, koans and stories from 25 centuries of awakened women.
The book is scheduled to be published by Wisdom Publications later in 2013.
And we are grateful to the generosity of editors Zenshin Florence Caplow and Reigetsu Susan Moon for making portions available for our study at Red Cedar Zen Community's 2013 winter practice period.
One of my favorite stories is about three monks on a pilgrimage.
Along the way, they met a woman who had a tea shop.
The woman prepared a pot of tea and brought three cups.
She said to them, "Oh monks, let those of you with miraculous powers drink tea."
The three looked at each other.
And the woman said, "Watch this decrepit old woman show her own miraculous powers."
Then she picked up the cups, poured the tea, and then went out.
Here is a story with many lessons for us.
Up front, we have the blind spots of the monks who are distracted by fears of not measuring up or not being well thought of.
And we have the courage shown by the woman in challenging norms of gender.
But then what?
Maybe besides the blind spot to what a miracle this everyday life is, they were also blind to the possibility of being guided in wisdom while stopping along the road for tea.
Or maybe then the monks have the courage to learn to be present with embarrassment and feelings of ignorance.
What would I do in that situation?
What do I do in that situation every day?
The effort to explore our blind spots is energized by bodhicitta.
The literal translation of bodhicitta is awakened heart, or awakening impulse.
Would you like all beings to be happy?
Apart from any benefit or detriment to yourself, do you have a desire for all beings to be happy?
Of course we do, and that fundamentally is bodhicitta.

That simple selfless desire for joy in the world is the foundation from which all practice springs forth, by the very act the sutras tell us of that desire arising within you for the benefit of others.
A causal chain is set in motion that leads to the liberation of all beings from suffering.
When such a desire arises for a glimpse of a moment in a human being, then 10,000 Buddhas in every atom raise a tremendous cry of celebration.
The hurrah rings out across the 10,000 universes in the ten directions.
Did you feel that happen just now when I asked you if you thought about others being happy?
It's true.
It's true.
Galen Godwin defines bodhicitta as the mind that wants to awaken to cause and effect, the mind that wants to awaken for the benefit of all beings.
The first step on that bodhisattva path, the first step in the liberation of all beings, is the simple blossom of bodhicitta available to us at any moment.
So you have this desire.
Then what?
Pema Chodron focuses on the aspect of not knowing nourished by bodhicitta.
From the desire, we can open to the possibility that the world is not as we know it to be.
When experience arises, we can move from predefined assumed associated thoughts, "Oh yes, I know this broken record," to look more closely with a willingness to see what we didn't before.
When meditation doesn't feel fresh, we can invite the possibility of seeing from a different perspective the thought that seems to match our memory.
We can invite in beginner's mind, not as a struggle or even an effort, but just a commitment to really look more closely at just what it is that's arising.
And if we misstep and fall into pattern thinking, okay, here's another opportunity right now to look more closely with the thought, "Maybe this isn't exactly what I expected it to be."
Some core concepts of Zen not to be overlooked in this study of blind spots in courage are non-duality and emptiness.
The teaching of non-duality challenges us to go beyond every observation we make, recognizing that it is not completely true and it is also not false.
There is not a solid line of separation between anything and its opposite.
Joan Tollefson summarizes that reality is completely inescapable and thus completely unattainable, for there is nothing apart from it to find it or lose it.
In response to the question of what non-duality is all about, she replies, "It is the dissolution of every answer to that question."
And there is diversity and variation in reality, but not separation.
Opposites are inseparable aspects of one whole.
She has to make that observation of dissolving all answers because no words can adequately describe the non-dual nature of reality.
For example, she uses the word inseparable, but for inseparable to have meaning, there must be separable.
While words cannot explain or answer, they can point.
They can direct us to a path which we can follow to familiarity with non-duality.
If you haven't read the Vimalakirti Sutra, I recommend it.
If nothing else, it is more entertaining than the Lotus or the Diamond Sutra.
And entertainment is the reason that we are practicing meditation, right?
It is amazing how we pay money to go see what is going on in other people's minds when there is so much happening right here.
The Sutra explores non-duality and the non-duality of non-duality.

The Vimalakirti Sutra plowed fresh ground as it spread in the second and third centuries of the common era with its teachings that not just monastics, but lay practitioners have the potential for great awakening.
The Sutra also took Shakyamuni Buddha's understated observation that there is not a difference between the sexes in capacity for enlightenment and greatly energized it into an asserted teaching.
In the Sutra, many of the familiar disciples of the Buddha have their blind spots illuminated.
Perhaps our greatest exposure to the teaching of emptiness is with the Heart Sutra.

Emptiness sounds scary, but when we chant Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva when deeply practicing Prajnaparamita, clearly saw that all five aggregates are empty and thus relieved all suffering, who is it that is practicing Prajnaparamita in this story?
As it's told, is it Shakyamuni Buddha?

No, the one deeply practicing Prajnaparamita, the discernment of form as emptiness and emptiness as form in this story is none other than the embodiment of compassion herself, Avalokiteshvara, Guan Yin.
When we cry for support from the one who hears the cries of the world, her infinite compassion offers us emptiness.
Maybe with trust in Guan Yin, we can summon the courage to let go of self.
The point in studying the Skandhas is that any place you go to identify yourself, what you find there is not you.
What you find there is in a transient state that came about because of many, many causes interacting, and what you find there fades into other conditions very quickly.
The same can be said for any other object you suppose exists in the world.
So here is a translation of the Skandhas that best capture the original intention for me this week: forms, judgment impulses, conceptions, mental patterns, and consciousness.
Forms, the physical world, empty.
Judgment impulses, that instantaneous initial reflex reaction to lean toward or away from any sensation, no self there.
Conceptions, the six senses, including what Buddhism identifies as the sense is the mind, what Buddhism identifies as the sense is the mind's identifying, recognizing, or naming.
Who is watching that?
Mental patterns, worry, appreciation, ideas, and decisions activated by inputs to the mind, nope, the self is not there.
And consciousness, the self is not just what watches someone planning the errands they're going to accomplish on break.
The emptiness of the Heart Sutra is sometimes translated as boundlessness because as it says, all these things in their own being are empty.
In other words, they're empty of isolation, empty of separateness.
That is why Guinyin practices emptiness, because it is the emptiness of being interconnected with all beings.
And then, what could there be but compassion?
At my home, we brought home a new puppy this week.
He's a Border Collie and Beauceron mix, a puppy with beginner's mind.
Our minds are often compared to a puppy, a puppy that needs to be trained, but that we need to be gentle with.
"Hey, what's that smell?
Oh gosh, it's dust under the furniture.
I love dust.
Amazing.
Wow, that bang across the street, that's scary."
Every few seconds, we need to bring the puppy back.
"Ah, the smell of rotting leaves.
Come on back.
I wonder what a nickel tastes like.
Come on back.
Catch the butterfly.
Come on back.
Lunch smells good.
Come on back."
I can't believe what my sister-in-law said during our last phone call.
"Come on back."
Then the puppy piddles on the carpet and everybody starts yelling.
The puppy of my mind is definitely like that.
But eventually, exploring and returning, exploring and returning, some new way of interacting with the world starts to jill.
Courage still requires effort, but it doesn't require patterns of stress.
Exploring what courage is, our class found a strong correlation with fear, moving forward in the presence of fear, or more accurately, not moving back, not stepping away or stepping to distraction.
Courage also connotes some element of risk, a strong example is the risk of exposing ourselves to others, or more powerful than that even, the risk of exposing ourselves to ourselves.
When Yuan was young, she decided not to marry or bear children, and she set her heart on the way of Chan.
She experienced a clear awakening at the words of Master Yuan Wu Kequan as he spoke to the assembly.
Yuan Wu is the teacher who compiled the Blue Cliff record.
Later Yuan Wu said to her, "You should go on to erase your views, then you will finally be free."
She answered in verse: "The pillar pulls out the bone sideways.
The void shows its claws and fangs.
Even if one profoundly understands, there is still sand in the eye."
Leaping to the heart of the koan, "Even if one profoundly understands, there is still sand in the eye."
In full awakening, old age, sickness and death still happen.
Greed, hate and delusion still happen.
There is grief and frustration and fear and anger, as well as desire, excitement and pleasure.
But we are not caught by them, we are free in them.
The Metta Sutta does not promise freedom from birth and death, but freedom from the duality of birth and death.
One tool for developing courage is developing equanimity.
Our lives are batted by gale force winds, pushing on us this way and that.
Equanimity is balance in the presence of the storm.
Equanimity is neither clinging nor pushing away.
Equanimity is not something we overtly do; it's not magic, it's not a rule that can be broken.
Equanimity arises with and through our practice of sitting.
For years, equanimity was mistranslated as indifference, which is actually opposite of what equanimity is.
Equanimity is being fully attentive to what's being thrown at us, not ignoring it, not distracting ourselves.
What does it mean to fully and deeply grieve without losing our presence of mind?

This investigation into courage and blind spots was inspired as I described in the way seeking mind talk, from an experience last year at Samish, I was eno for a ceremony to present the names of the women ancestors to those who had previously undertaken Jukai.
Due to miscommunications or other errors, that ceremony didn't play out as planned.
It ended up being short, disjointed, and severely understated.

The ceremony was supposed to be a long overdue recognition and celebration of the impact our women ancestors have had on our practice, and it ended up offending some of the people it should have been honoring.
This ceremony honoring women leaders was planned out and implemented by three men, guiding teacher Norman, spiritual director Tim, and me as eno, without women's input.
Being grateful to the women who had the courage to point out our blind spots, these topics of courage and blind spots cried out for further study.
Often in Zen, problems appear to get worse when we bring them into our practice.
They are not really stronger, but we see them more clearly.
One of the biggest examples is how busy our mind is.
The busy mind seems to be so much more noticeable if we have been sitting a little bit.
Similarly, the more you look for blind spots, the more you'll find.
One tool we found helpful in the class was to try to identify and name blind spots in others so that we can turn right around and ask, "How does this blind spot manifest itself in my actions?"
One of my friends at work, Dan, is retiring this month.
We're all very happy for him.
Kevin says that Dan deserves a big going away party, that we should all bring all of our families and take Dan out to a nice restaurant.
Kevin is right that Dan deserves a great honor.
Dan has always been there for anyone who needed his help.
He has mentored all of us without ever speaking an unkind word about anyone.
But then there's Patrick.
Patrick says that's not what Dan wants.
Dan is shy and very uncomfortable when he's the center of attention.
Patrick says Dan would really rather that we just get our close work crew together and have some cake at the break table.
Kevin thinks that Patrick is selfish for doing so little for Dan after Dan has given so much to us.
Patrick thinks that Kevin is selfish for not doing what it is that Dan wants.
Both of them are walking away mad, unwilling to do anything further.
There's some very different views of the situation.
Enough blind spots for all.
That sure is me often just not seeing the other point of view, not even open to the possibility that I might not be seeing everything clearly.
Throughout this talk, the names have been changed by the way.
What is the medicine for these blind spots?
I joked in the class that it sounds like a disease.
What's the prognosis, doctor?
The test results indicate you have blind spots.
Is it serious?
Well, there's no cure, but with the proper regimen most patients are able to live a more joyful life.
Take three refuges and call me in the morning.
It takes awareness of Buddha to penetrate our blind spots, and that we developed by practicing Dharma on and off the cushion.
And finding our blind spots is mostly impossible without help from our community, from our Sangha.
Bodhidharma was a monk who ventured from India to China to teach Buddhism.
In his words, "To rescue the deluded by transmitting the Dharma."
Bodhidharma had four disciples, the most famous of whom is Huike.
Another of his disciples is the nun called Zongqi.
One day Bodhidharma called his students together and asked them to describe their practice realization.
Zongqi's response, "My understanding now is that it is like the joy of seeing the eastern pure land of Akshobya Buddha.
It is felt at the first glance, but not the second glance."
"It is felt at the first glance, but not at the second glance."
To me, that refers to the experience of joy or fear or any other Skandha arising.
We are truly present with it in the arising, and with the transient changing nature of all phenomena.
If we try to grasp it, try to get a second glance, now we're creating suffering.

Our effort on the cushion is carried into the every day of our lives, having the courage to meet what is truly present, not what we assume is present based on our memories and beliefs, but what presents itself now.
That is the lighthearted engagement we are capable of.
This practice with courage has effects.
When courage is mixed into the karmic causal chain, the world is changed.
We talk a lot about causation in our study of the self.
We can witness examples of causation happen, but the bulk of the body of karma is far beyond our perception.
The basics of our practice are the soil for courage to arise and for becoming aware of and feeling out the contents of our blind spots.
We start with posture.
On that foundation is the recognition of phenomena as they arise and pass away.
Phenomena including thinking, attachment, desire, our breath, pain.
So gently we return, we return, we return, always with the openness, with the question, "Despite my questions, despite my preconceptions, what is this really?"

Due to miscommunications or other errors, that ceremony didn't play out as planned. It ended up being short, disjointed, and severely understated. The ceremony was supposed to be a long overdue recognition and celebration

of the impact our women ancestors have had on our practice. And it ended up offending some of the people it should have been honoring. This ceremony honoring women leaders was planned out and implemented by three men, guiding teacher Norman, spiritual director Tim, and me as eno, without women's input. Being grateful to the women who had the courage to point out our blind spots, these topics of courage and blind spots cried out for further study. Often in Zen, problems appear to get worse when we bring them into our practice.

They are not really stronger, but we see them more clearly. One of the biggest examples is how busy our mind is. The busy mind seems to be so much more noticeable if we have been sitting a little bit. Similarly, the more you look for blind spots, the more you'll find. One tool we found helpful in the class was to try to identify and name blind spots in others so that we can turn right around and ask, how does this blind spot manifest itself in my actions? One of my friends at work, Dan, is retiring this month.

We're all very happy for him. Kevin says that Dan deserves a big going away party, that we should all bring all of our families and take Dan out to a nice restaurant. Kevin is right that Dan deserves a great honor. Dan has always been there for anyone who needed his help. He has mentored all of us without ever speaking an unkind word about anyone. But then there's Patrick. Patrick says that's not what Dan wants.

Dan is shy and very uncomfortable when he's the center of attention. Patrick says Dan would really rather that we just get our close work crew together and have some cake at the break table. Kevin thinks that Patrick is selfish for doing so little for Dan after Dan has given so much to us. Patrick thinks that Kevin is selfish for not doing what it is that Dan wants. Both of them are walking away mad, unwilling to do anything further. There's some very different views of the situation.

Enough blind spots for all. That sure is me often just not seeing the other point of view, not even open to the possibility that I might not be seeing everything clearly. Throughout this talk the names have been changed by the way. What is the medicine for these blind spots? I joked in the class that it sounds like a disease. What's the prognosis doctor? The test results indicate you have blind spots.

Is it serious? Well, there's no cure, but with the proper regimen most patients are able to live a more joyful life. Take three refuges and call me in the morning. It takes awareness of Buddha to penetrate our blind spots. And that we developed by practicing Dharma on and off the cushion. And finding our blind spots is mostly impossible without help from our community, from our Sangha. Bodhidharma was a monk who ventured from India to China to teach Buddhism.

In his words, to rescue the deluded by transmitting the Dharma. Bodhidharma had four disciples, the most famous of whom is Huike. Another of his disciples is the nun called Zongqi. One day Bodhidharma called his students together and asked them to describe their practice realization. Zongqi's response, My understanding now is that it is like the joy of seeing the eastern pure land of Akshobya Buddha. It is felt at the first glance, but not the second glance.

It is felt at the first glance, but not at the second glance. To me, that refers to the experience of joy or fear or any other Skandha arising. We are truly present with it in the arising. And with the transient changing nature of all phenomena. If we try to grasp it, try to get a second glance, now we're creating suffering. Our effort on the cushion is carried into the every day of our lives. Having the courage to meet what is truly present. Not what we assume is present based on our memories and beliefs, but what presents itself now.

That is the lighthearted engagement we are capable of. This practice with courage has effects. When courage is mixed into the karmic causal chain, the world is changed. We talk a lot about causation in our study of the self. We can witness examples of causation happen, but the bulk of the body of karma is far beyond our perception. The basics of our practice are the soil for courage to arise and for becoming aware of and feeling out the contents of our blind spots.

We start with posture. On that foundation is the recognition of phenomena as they arise and pass away. Phenomena including thinking, attachment, desire, our breath, pain. So gently we return, we return, we return. Always with the openness, with the question, despite my questions, despite my preconceptions, what is this really?
